report:
**Conclusion: No — saw palmetto does not improve BPH symptoms long-term beyond placebo.**

The evidence strongly supports the "no" answer. The landmark STEP trial (NEJM, 2006), a year-long randomized double-blind placebo-controlled study, found that saw palmetto was not superior to placebo for improving urinary symptoms or objective measures of BPH. The subsequent CAMUS trial (Barry et al., JAMA, 2011), a large NIH-funded U.S./Canadian trial, escalated doses up to three times the standard 320 mg/day over 18 months and still found no significant benefit over placebo for symptom improvement—though it confirmed safety.

The Cochrane systematic review (Tacklind et al.) concluded that Serenoa repens, even at double and triple doses, did not improve urinary flow measures or prostate size in men with BPH-related lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS). A 2024 AAFP evidence summary explicitly states: "Saw palmetto, alone or in combination with other phytotherapeutic agents, does not improve urologic symptoms or quality of life in the short term (3 to 6 months) or long term (12 to 17 months)." A 2025 comprehensive review similarly reports high-certainty evidence of no clinically meaningful benefit at both short- and long-term follow-up, with adverse event rates comparable to placebo.

While some older meta-analyses and European trials suggested modest benefits, the highest-quality, largest, and most recent placebo-controlled trials and systematic reviews consistently show no meaningful advantage over placebo.
